# Inlining

Inlining is driven by a call graph, constructed from the program's static call sites with nodes as procedures (or SCCs of mutually recursive procedures) and edges as call sites, annotated with callee candidates (possibly a set, when indirect/virtual calls require resolution). The order in which this graph is traversed matters: bottom-up inlining processes callees before callers, following a reverse topological order of the SCC-condensed call graph. This lets the compiler first finish optimizing and measuring the size/cost of a callee so that when it's considered for inlining into a caller, its post-optimization cost is known rather than estimated from an unoptimized body. Bottom-up order also naturally supports iterative growth: a leaf procedure gets inlined into its callers, those callers grow and may themselves become inlining candidates further up, which is how bottom-up inlining achieves transitive flattening of shallow call chains without needing a separate fixed-point pass over the whole program. Top-down inlining instead processes callers before callees, which is cheaper to drive from an interprocedural analysis that propagates context (e.g., argument constants) downward, but risks inlining a callee whose body hasn't yet benefited from simplification, inflating code size estimates. Most production compilers (LLVM, GCC) use primarily bottom-up strategies with worklist-based iteration over the SCC DAG, re-enqueuing callers after callees are finalized.

Decisions to inline rely on a cost model. LLVM's `InlineCost` analysis walks the callee's IR and accumulates a synthetic "cost" by assigning weights to instructions, subtracting "bonuses" for simplifications that inlining is expected to unlock (e.g., a call argument that's a constant feeding a branch, enabling branch folding; a GEP with constant offsets collapsing; vector/SIMD-friendly code). This is combined with a size threshold (`-inline-threshold`, tunable, with different defaults for `-O2`/`-O3`/`-Oz`), and special-cased bonuses for single-call-site callees (cost reduced toward "always inline" since there's no duplication penalty) and callees marked `alwaysinline`/`noinline` as hard overrides. GCC's inliner similarly computes a per-callee badness/benefit score, but exposes a larger set of `--param` knobs directly: `max-inline-insns-auto`, `max-inline-insns-single`, `inline-unit-growth`, `large-function-growth`, each bounding different aspects — single callee size, aggregate growth of a translation unit, and growth of any one caller — reflecting a multi-constraint budget rather than one scalar threshold. Both models are heuristic rather than provably optimal because the true benefit of inlining (enabling downstream optimization) is only knowable after running those optimizations, which is too expensive to do speculatively for every candidate.

Devirtualization-enabled inlining targets virtual/indirect calls, which ordinary inlining can't touch because the callee isn't statically known. Class hierarchy analysis (CHA) is a whole-program interprocedural analysis that, assuming a closed class hierarchy (no further subclassing, often valid after whole-program/LTO analysis or in sealed/final contexts), determines that a virtual call site has only one possible target (monomorphic) and converts it to a direct call, which can then be inlined normally. When the hierarchy isn't closed or CHA proves polymorphism, compilers use speculative/guarded devirtualization: insert a runtime type check (e.g., compare the vtable pointer or class ID against the expected type) guarding an inlined fast path for the common case, with a fallback to the original indirect call. This pattern — "if (typecheck) inlined-direct-call else indirect-call" — trades a branch for the chance to inline the hot path. In JIT contexts (V8, HotSpot), this is driven by type feedback collected at runtime via inline caches (ICs): a monomorphic IC records a single observed receiver type/shape at a call site and the JIT compiler bakes a guard against that type with inlining behind it; a polymorphic IC records a handful of observed types (typically 2-4) and compiles a guard chain or dispatches accordingly; beyond that it degrades to a megamorphic IC, usually precluding inlining and falling back to a general dispatch stub. These feedback-driven decisions are speculative and require deoptimization support: if an assumption is violated at runtime, the JIT must bail out from optimized code back to a baseline/interpreter tier (on-stack replacement or deopt).

Partial inlining addresses large callees with a cold region (e.g., error handling, rare branches) by splitting the callee into a small hot "stub" and a cold outlined remainder, inlining only the stub at the call site while leaving a call to the outlined cold part. This captures most of the benefit (eliminating call overhead, enabling constant propagation through the hot path) without the code-size blowup of inlining the whole body. LLVM implements this as part of its inliner pass using an explicit cold-region outlining transform guided by profile data (block frequencies) to decide what counts as cold.

Recursive calls require bounded recursive inlining: the inliner may inline a self-recursive call a fixed number of levels (a factor controlled by recursion-depth parameters) to unroll shallow recursion into straight-line or loop code, but must terminate — naive inlining of a recursive call graph diverges, so the compiler tracks inlining depth per call-site chain and refuses further inlining past a cap, or disallows inlining recursive calls altogether except for tail-recursive patterns better handled by tail-call optimization.

Finally, inlining interacts tightly with other optimizations in a feedback loop often summarized as "inline then clean up": inlining alone usually doesn't improve performance until followed by constant propagation, sparse conditional constant propagation, dead code elimination, and CSE operating across the newly merged scope — e.g., a callee's parameter becomes a caller-side constant post-inlining, enabling branch folding and further DCE of now-unreachable code, which shrinks the inlined body back down, sometimes below the original cost estimate. This is why inliners' cost models try to award bonus credit for "this argument is constant" ahead of time — to approximate the benefit that will only materialize after the subsequent cleanup pass runs.

# Register Allocation

Graph-coloring register allocation, as formalized by Chaitin and refined by Briggs, models the allocation problem as coloring an interference graph: nodes are live ranges (virtual registers), edges connect live ranges simultaneously live at some program point (hence requiring distinct physical registers), and a k-coloring (k = number of physical registers) is sought. The Chaitin-Briggs algorithm proceeds in phases: build constructs the interference graph from liveness analysis; simplify repeatedly removes nodes of degree < k (such nodes are "trivially colorable" — guaranteed colorable regardless of neighbors' colors) and pushes them onto a stack; when no such node exists, spill selects a node (by estimated spill cost) to mark as a potential spill and removes it optimistically (Briggs's refinement is to *not* immediately commit to spilling — this node is pushed anyway as an "optimistic spill candidate" and only materializes as an actual spill if, upon select, no color remains); select pops the stack and assigns colors greedily, actually spilling (inserting loads/stores and creating a new live range) only if a popped node truly has no free color among its already-colored neighbors. Coalescing merges the live ranges of a move instruction's source and destination to eliminate the move, but naive (aggressive) coalescing can increase degree and reduce colorability; Briggs's conservative coalescing only merges two nodes if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k, preserving colorability guarantees, while Chaitin's original (more aggressive) criterion merges whenever the combined node's neighbor set size is < k, which is sound but less conservative and can induce more spilling in adversarial cases. The algorithm iterates build-simplify-spill-select across spill rounds since inserting spill code changes liveness.

Linear scan register allocation sidesteps full graph construction. Live ranges are computed and sorted by start point, then scanned in a single linear pass, maintaining an active set of live ranges currently assigned registers; when a new range begins and no register is free, the range with the furthest-away next use (or in older formulations, the one ending latest) is spilled. This is asymptotically cheaper than graph coloring (near-linear vs. the graph-coloring's higher practical cost from iterative interference-graph rebuilding) and is the method of choice for JITs under compile-time pressure. V8's allocator historically used a second-chance binpacking variant: rather than committing a spill decision permanently, a range that's evicted gets a "second chance" — it can be reloaded into a register later if one frees up, effectively splitting its lifetime into disjoint sub-intervals handled independently, which approximates some of the benefit of live-range splitting without full SSA-based range analysis.

SSA-based register allocation, formalized by Hack, Grund, and Goos, exploits a key structural property: the interference graph of a program in strict SSA form (with values live across control-flow merges represented via φ-functions) is a chordal graph — every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord. Chordal graphs are colorable in polynomial time optimally via a perfect elimination ordering (computable by maximum cardinality search), meaning the NP-hard general graph-coloring problem becomes tractable exactly, not just heuristically, when restricted to SSA-form interference graphs. This gives a principled algorithm: compute the perfect elimination order, color in that order, and the result is provably optimal for pure register assignment, modulo the fact that φ-function placement and coalescing after SSA destruction can reintroduce complications; pre-coloring due to calling-convention constraints also requires care within this framework.

Live range splitting addresses the fact that a long-lived virtual register may only need a physical register for parts of its live range; splitting divides one live range into several at insertion of copy instructions, so that the value can reside in different physical registers (or spill to memory) over different sub-ranges, reducing interference-graph degree and the cost of spilling (a spilled sub-range need not cover the register's entire lifetime). Spill cost estimation weighs, per candidate for spilling, the estimated runtime execution frequency of its definitions/uses (often loop-nesting-depth-weighted, since a spill inside a loop executes on every iteration) against the degree-reduction benefit of removing it from the interference graph, guiding spill selection to minimize expected dynamic load/store overhead rather than static instruction count.

PBQP-based allocation reformulates register allocation (including architecture-specific constraints like register pairs, aliasing, or operand co-location requirements that aren't naturally expressible as simple graph coloring) as a partitioned boolean quadratic program: each live range gets a cost vector over possible colors (including a spill option), and each interference edge gets a cost matrix penalizing incompatible color assignments; the PBQP solver (via reduction rules — simplifying degree-1/degree-2 nodes similarly to graph-coloring's simplify phase, falling back to heuristic branch-and-bound for irreducible cases) finds a low-cost assignment. This generalizes Chaitin-Briggs by allowing arbitrary pairwise costs, making it well-suited to targets with irregular register constraints (e.g., some DSPs, or architectures with overlapping/aliased register files) where plain k-coloring's uniform "any register works" assumption breaks down.

# Instruction Scheduling

Instruction scheduling reorders instructions within a scope (basic block, or more broadly a region) to maximize pipeline/functional-unit utilization and hide latency, subject to correctness constraints encoded in a data-dependence graph (DDG). The DDG has nodes for instructions and edges for dependencies: true dependencies (read-after-write, RAW, where a later instruction reads a value a prior one writes — a genuine dataflow dependency that scheduling can never violate), anti-dependencies (write-after-read, WAR, where a later write would clobber a value an earlier instruction still needs to read — this is a false dependency arising from register/storage reuse, removable by renaming), and output dependencies (write-after-write, WAW, two writes to the same location whose relative order must be preserved for correctness of whichever read observes the final value, again a reuse artifact removable by renaming). Only RAW edges reflect true dataflow; WAR/WAW are name-dependence hazards that register renaming (either in hardware, out-of-order cores, or statically by the compiler assigning fresh virtual registers) can eliminate, widening the scheduler's freedom. Each DDG edge is typically annotated with a latency (minimum cycle delay between issuing the source and being allowed to issue the sink).

List scheduling is the workhorse heuristic: starting from the DDG, maintain a ready list of instructions whose predecessors have all been scheduled, and repeatedly pick the highest-priority ready instruction to schedule next, advancing a notional clock subject to latency and resource constraints (functional unit availability, issue width). Priority functions commonly use critical-path scheduling: prioritize instructions by their distance-to-end on the longest weighted path through the DDG (sometimes called the "height" or computed via the time a node would execute if scheduled ASAP subject only to latency, ignoring resource limits) — scheduling critical-path instructions earliest prevents them from later delaying the schedule's end. This is closely related to the classical ASAP/ALAP bounds: ASAP (as-soon-as-possible) scheduling assigns each node the earliest cycle consistent with its predecessors' latencies, giving a lower bound on completion for every node and defining the minimal schedule length ignoring resources; ALAP (as-late-as-possible) assigns each node the latest cycle consistent with not delaying the overall schedule beyond that minimal length, working backward from the sinks. The difference ALAP − ASAP per node is its slack; zero-slack nodes lie on the critical path and are prioritized first in list scheduling, since delaying them delays the whole schedule, while high-slack nodes can be moved opportunistically to fill resource gaps.

Basic-block scheduling confines reordering to within a single block (no control-flow-exiting instructions crossed), which is simple and safe but limits opportunity, especially for blocks too short to hide multi-cycle latencies (e.g., a load-use latency that the block ends before resolving). Global scheduling extends movement across block boundaries. Trace scheduling, introduced by Fisher, selects a trace — a frequently executed, acyclic sequence of basic blocks determined via profile data or heuristics (effectively the predicted hot path through branches) — and schedules it as if it were one large basic block, moving instructions across the original block boundaries within the trace. Because the trace isn't the only possible control-flow path, this requires compensation code: when an instruction is moved above a branch that can exit the trace, correctness on the off-trace path requires inserting a corrective copy of that instruction (or an undo) on the side-entrance/side-exit edges, so that semantics are preserved regardless of which path is actually taken at runtime. This trades code growth and compensation overhead for improved scheduling on the (hopefully dominant) hot trace.

Software pipelining targets loops directly, overlapping iterations so that different pipeline stages of consecutive iterations execute concurrently, maximizing steady-state throughput. Modulo scheduling is the standard formalization: the loop body is scheduled within a single period called the initiation interval (II) — the number of cycles between successive iteration starts — such that resource usage and dependency latencies are satisfied modulo II (i.e., the same schedule repeats every II cycles, with operations from different iterations interleaved in the hardware pipeline simultaneously). The minimum achievable II (MII) is computed as the maximum of two lower bounds: the resource-constrained MII (ResMII), the ceiling of (total usage of the most contended functional unit per iteration) divided by (number of units of that type available), and the recurrence-constrained MII (RecMII), the maximum over all cyclic dependence chains (loop-carried dependencies) of (total latency around the cycle) divided by (number of iterations the cycle spans), since a dependency cycle enforces a minimum spacing regardless of resources. The scheduler iterates increasing candidate II starting from MII until a feasible modulo schedule is found (via modulo variants of list scheduling respecting modulo resource reservation tables). The resulting pipelined loop needs a prologue (ramp-up code filling the pipeline before steady state, executing partial iterations' early stages), the steady-state kernel (the single repeating II-cycle body, doing work for several overlapping iterations at once), and an epilogue (ramp-down, draining the pipeline's in-flight iterations after the loop's trip count is exhausted) — the classic kernel/prologue/epilogue structure.

VLIW scheduling constraints are distinctive because a VLIW (very long instruction word) architecture exposes instruction-level parallelism explicitly in the encoding: the compiler, not hardware, must pack multiple independent operations into each wide instruction bundle respecting fixed per-bundle slot constraints (e.g., exactly one branch slot, a fixed number of ALU/load-store slots), with no hardware interlocking to dynamically stall on hazards — meaning the scheduler must statically guarantee latency correctness (if a result isn't ready, the compiler must not issue the dependent op early; there's no scoreboard to catch it) and must respect that unfilled slots in a bundle are wasted (no-ops), making bundle-packing density itself an optimization objective tightly coupled with the list-scheduling/modulo-scheduling algorithms used to fill them.

# Loop Vectorization

## Dependence analysis as the legality gate

Before any vectorization transform fires, the compiler must establish that reordering or grouping iterations does not change program semantics. The standard formalism is the distance vector and direction vector representation of dependences between array references across loop nests. For a dependence from statement S1 (iteration i) to S2 (iteration j), the distance vector component is j−i for each loop level, and the direction vector records sign(j−i) ∈ {<, =, >}. A dependence is loop-carried at level k if the direction vector's first nonzero (non-"=") entry occurs at level k; loop-independent dependences occur within a single iteration.

For single-dimension affine subscripts of the form a·i + b accessed at two points, the GCD test checks necessary (not sufficient) conditions for dependence existence: a dependence can exist only if gcd(a1, a2) divides (b2 − b1); if it doesn't divide evenly, no integer solution exists and the references are proven independent. The GCD test is cheap but imprecise — it ignores loop bounds, so it can report "may depend" when the true index set admits no solution within bounds.

The Banerjee test tightens this by using the loop bounds to compute, for a linear subscript expression, the interval of possible values of the dependence distance (treating loop index differences as bounded real variables) and checking whether zero (or the required direction) falls within that interval. It operates separately on the "positive part" and "negative part" of coefficients to get extremal bounds, and is exact for single coefficients but, like most practical tests, inexact for general multi-dimensional affine systems. For vectorization specifically, the critical loop-carried dependence case is distance vectors with a nonzero distance at the loop being vectorized: a "<" direction at that level (source iteration precedes sink) is vectorization-hostile if the distance is smaller than the vector length, because it means an iteration depends on a result not yet produced within the same vector group. A distance-vector dependence with direction "=" at the vectorized level (loop-independent within an iteration) is harmless to vectorization. This is the formal underpinning of the common informal rule "no self-recurrence across loop iterations" that vectorizing compilers check.

## LLVM's Loop Vectorizer: strip-mining, VF, and UF

LLVM's Loop Vectorizer (and similarly GCC's) implements SIMDization via strip-mining: the original scalar loop with trip count N is transformed into an outer loop that processes chunks of VF iterations using vector instructions operating on VF-wide SIMD registers, plus a scalar remainder loop (or masked tail) to handle N mod VF leftover iterations. The vectorization factor VF is chosen based on the target's vector register width and the element type's bit width — e.g., 128-bit SSE registers vectorizing 32-bit floats give VF=4; AVX-512 with the same type gives VF=16. VF selection also accounts for "shrinking" element types inside the loop body (e.g., if a comparison truncates to i8, a larger VF may be legal and profitable for that portion, handled via LLVM's notion of "vectorizing with a VF per type" in some passes).

Orthogonally, LLVM introduces an interleaving factor UF (unroll factor), where the vectorized body is itself unrolled UF times, interleaving UF independent vector-register streams. This increases instruction-level parallelism to hide vector instruction latency and amortize loop overhead (branch, induction variable update) across more work, independent of the SIMD width decision. The two factors multiply: each outer-loop iteration of the transformed loop consumes VF × UF original scalar iterations. The Loop Vectorizer's cost model separately searches over candidate VFs and UFs, estimating cycles for each combination using the target's TargetTransformInfo cost tables (per-instruction throughput/latency, shuffle costs, memory access costs including gather/scatter penalties), and picks the combination minimizing estimated cost per scalar element, subject to register pressure constraints (the product VF×UF must not force excessive spilling).

## Handling reductions

A reduction variable is one updated each iteration by a commutative-and-associative operator (sum, product, min/max, bitwise and/or/xor) using only its own prior value and loop-invariant/independent inputs — formally, a scalar recurrence of the form acc = acc OP f(i) with no other use of acc inside the loop body except through that recurrence. Reduction variable recognition (an idiom-recognition analysis, often built on LLVM's ScalarEvolution or a dedicated reduction-detection pass) identifies the PHI node forming the cyclic use-def chain and classifies the operator.

Because the floating-point version of such an operator is not strictly associative (rounding), reduction vectorization under strict IEEE semantics requires either a relaxed floating-point mode (e.g., `-ffast-math`, or explicit `#pragma clang loop vectorize` combined with fast-math function attributes) or restricting vectorization to reduction operators that remain exactly associative for the element type (integer add, bitwise ops). Given a sanctioned associative operator, vectorization computes VF partial accumulators in a vector register — each lane accumulating every VF-th original iteration's contribution — and after the strip-mined loop concludes, performs a horizontal reduction (a vector reduction idiom) that collapses the vector accumulator to a scalar, using a log2(VF)-step shuffle-and-op tree, or a dedicated hardware instruction where available (e.g., `vhaddps`, or LLVM's `llvm.vector.reduce.*` intrinsics which lower to target-specific reduction sequences). This changes the order of summation relative to the scalar loop, which is the formal source of the floating-point non-bit-exactness tradeoff.

## Predication (if-conversion) for control flow

Loops containing conditional statements (an `if` inside the loop body) cannot be vectorized directly because different lanes of a SIMD group would need to take different control paths. The standard technique is if-conversion: the conditional is converted into straight-line code where the side-effecting operations are predicated/masked by the boolean condition, rather than guarded by a branch. Concretely, `if (c) a[i] = x;` becomes a masked store (or a select feeding an unconditional store) where only lanes with c=true commit their result. On targets without hardware masking (older SSE), this is emulated via blend/select instructions that compute both the "then" and "else" values for all lanes and select per-lane; on targets with mask registers (AVX-512, SVE, RISC-V V) it compiles directly to predicated vector instructions, avoiding wasted computation and problematic side effects (e.g., avoiding a masked-out lane from faulting on an out-of-bounds load, which requires additional care — masked loads/stores with fault suppression, or speculation-safety analysis).

## Loop peeling, versioning, and runtime checks

Loop peeling strips off a prefix (and/or suffix) of iterations to run scalar, commonly to force the remaining loop body to start at a memory-aligned boundary so the vectorized body can use aligned vector loads/stores instead of slower unaligned accesses — this is alignment peeling. Separately, loop versioning for aliasing addresses the common case where the compiler cannot statically prove that two pointer-based array accesses (e.g., `a[i]` and `b[i]` where a and b are runtime pointers) don't overlap. The compiler emits a runtime pointer aliasing check (e.g., checking that the address ranges [a, a+N) and [b, b+N) don't intersect) and generates two versions of the loop: a vectorized fast path taken when the check proves non-aliasing, and a safe scalar (or non-vectorized) fallback otherwise. This is a form of speculative optimization with a correctness-preserving guard, distinct from speculation that requires rollback — here the two versions are simply alternate statically-compiled paths selected at runtime.

## Cost modeling

Vectorization is not always profitable: small trip counts amortize poorly against the strip-mine/remainder-loop overhead, gather/scatter for non-unit-stride access is expensive, and inserted mask/blend/shuffle instructions for if-converted or misaligned code can exceed the savings from SIMD width. Production vectorizers (LLVM's Loop Vectorizer, GCC's tree-vectorizer) build an explicit cost model: each candidate instruction gets a target-specific cost (reciprocal throughput cycles typically), summed across the loop body for each candidate (VF, UF) pair, and compared against the scalar loop's cost scaled by VF. Vectorization proceeds only if the vector cost per original iteration beats the scalar cost per iteration by a margin, and the compiler may additionally consult the trip count (if known or bounded) to amortize the strip-mine preamble/epilogue overhead — this is why `#pragma clang loop vectorize(enable)` exists, to override the cost model's conservative judgment on loops where profiling or programmer knowledge indicates profitability that static cost estimation misjudges.

# General Loop Optimizations

## Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)

LICM identifies computations inside a loop body whose operands are all loop-invariant — defined outside the loop, or themselves recomputed identically every iteration — and hoists them to the loop preheader, a dedicated basic block inserted immediately before the loop header that executes exactly once before entering the loop. The analysis is a straightforward dataflow formulation: an instruction is invariant if all its operands are either defined outside the loop or are themselves invariant instructions already hoisted (a fixpoint computation over the use-def chains restricted to the loop body). Correctness requires more than invariance, however: for instructions with side effects or exception/trap behavior (loads that might fault, calls, divisions that might trap on divide-by-zero), the compiler must also prove the instruction is safe to speculate — i.e., that it would execute on every path through the loop anyway (or use must-execute / control-dependence analysis), otherwise hoisting could introduce a trap on a path that originally avoided it. For memory operations specifically, LICM of loads requires alias analysis to prove no intervening store in the loop can alias the hoisted load's address (and conversely, store sinking, hoisting a redundant store to after the loop, requires proving the stored location isn't observed mid-loop by an aliasing load). LICM is foundational because it also enables and interacts with strength reduction and is typically run both before and after other loop transformations in a compiler's pass pipeline since those transformations often expose new invariant subexpressions.

## Induction variable analysis and strength reduction

A loop's canonical induction variable is a variable that is initialized before the loop and incremented by a fixed constant exactly once per iteration (the classic `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` counter), forming the simplest basis for all other induction variables in the loop. Linear induction variable recognition generalizes this: a variable V is a linear function of the canonical IV if it can be expressed as V = c1·i + c0 for loop-invariant c1, c0, even if it's updated by its own increment statement rather than computed directly from i each time (e.g., a pointer `p` incremented by a constant stride each iteration tracking array traversal in lockstep with `i`). Compilers typically normalize this reasoning using a chain-of-recurrences or closed-form representation — LLVM's ScalarEvolution analysis represents such variables as `{start, +, step}<loop>` expressions, enabling uniform reasoning about all induction variables in a loop regardless of surface syntactic form.

Strength reduction exploits this: if a derived value inside the loop is computed by an expensive operation (multiplication, or repeated array-indexing address computation involving a multiply by element size) but is linear in the induction variable, the compiler replaces the per-iteration multiply with a per-iteration addition of the precomputed step, carrying the value forward across iterations instead of recomputing it from scratch — e.g., replacing `a[i*4]`'s address computation `base + i*4*sizeof(elt)` with an incrementally updated pointer `p += stride` each iteration. This trades a multiply for an add, which was historically a much cheaper operation and remains useful for reducing critical-path latency and enabling simpler addressing modes. After strength reduction, a final pass (induction variable elimination / linear function test replacement) may eliminate the original canonical IV entirely if the loop's exit test and all uses can be rewritten in terms of a surviving derived induction variable, reducing register pressure and instruction count.

## Loop unrolling and its interaction with scheduling

Full unrolling replaces a loop with a fixed, statically known trip count by the literal sequential repetition of its body that many times, eliminating loop control overhead (branch, counter increment, exit test) entirely and exposing cross-iteration instruction scheduling opportunities to the backend scheduler. Partial unrolling instead replicates the body a chosen unroll factor U times inside a loop that now increments by U per iteration, with a remainder loop (or peeled/masked tail) handling trip counts not evenly divisible by U — structurally identical to the strip-mining pattern used in vectorization, but motivated by scalar instruction-level parallelism and amortizing loop overhead rather than SIMD lane-width packing.

The deep interaction with instruction scheduling is the primary reason unrolling helps on pipelined/superscalar/VLIW targets: a single iteration's body often has a short dependence chain with latency that stalls the pipeline waiting for results, but after unrolling, the scheduler can interleave independent operations from multiple unrolled copies to fill those stall cycles, since different unrolled iterations are (for the common strength-reduced/vectorizable case) mutually independent. This is closely related to, and often paired with, software pipelining (modulo scheduling), where instead of literally duplicating code the compiler constructs a new steady-state loop body that overlaps the execution of an iteration's tail with the next iteration's head, forming a stable schedule repeated every iteration; unrolling is the cheaper, simpler (if code-size-costlier) alternative that achieves similar latency-hiding without needing the more complex prologue/epilogue construction that software pipelining requires.

## Loop fusion and fission (distribution)

Loop fusion merges two (or more) adjacent loops with the same iteration space (or compatible bounds, possibly after guard/trip-count equalization) into a single loop body executing both original bodies' statements per iteration. This reduces loop control overhead, and more importantly can improve data locality by combining loops that touch the same array — rather than one loop streaming through array A to completion and a later loop re-streaming through A, fusion interleaves the accesses so data loaded for one loop's use is still cache-resident for the other's use in the same iteration. Fusion's legality condition is governed by dependence direction vectors between the two loops: fusion is illegal if it would reverse the direction of some dependence relative to the original program order, specifically if loop 1 at iteration j depends on loop 2's result from some iteration i < j (a dependence that pointed "forward across loops" becomes, after fusion, a backward same-iteration or later-iteration dependence violating the original ordering — formally fusion-preventing when it creates a negative distance dependence that didn't exist in the fused direction).

Fission (distribution) is the inverse: splitting one loop's body into multiple separate loops, each executing a subset of the original statements over the same iteration space. This is useful when the combined body has no exploitable locality benefit, but can be fissioned so that different sub-loops become independently vectorizable (one might have a vectorization-blocking recurrence while another doesn't), or to reduce register pressure within a single iteration (fewer live values at once when work is split). Fission's legality similarly requires that no dependence crosses from a statement assigned to a later sub-loop back to a statement assigned to an earlier sub-loop at an earlier iteration, i.e., splitting must respect the partial order imposed by the original dependence graph.

## Loop interchange and tiling for locality

Loop interchange swaps the nesting order of two loops in a perfectly (or imperfectly, with additional care) nested loop structure — e.g., converting a row-major traversal of a column-major-stored array into a loop order that matches memory layout, turning stride-N accesses into stride-1 accesses and converting poor spatial locality into good spatial locality (fewer cache lines touched per unit of useful work, better prefetcher behavior). Legality is governed by the direction vectors of carried dependences across the two loops being swapped: interchange is legal only if it does not reverse any dependence into an "illegal" direction — concretely, a dependence with direction vector having a ">" in the position of the loop being moved outward combined with "<" in the inner position (or more generally, any direction vector where interchanging the two components would produce a direction vector that is not lexicographically non-negative in the new order) blocks the transformation, since it would mean a later iteration's value is consumed before it's produced under the new order.

Loop tiling (blocking) partitions the iteration space of one or more loops into fixed-size rectangular (in general, affine) blocks, restructuring e.g. a doubly nested loop over an N×N array into an additional pair of outer loops stepping by tile size T and inner loops of size T traversing within each tile. The goal is to shrink the working set touched between reuses of a given cache line down to the tile's footprint so that it fits within a target cache level, converting what would otherwise be capacity-miss-dominated reuse (useful data evicted before it's reused, because the full array doesn't fit in cache) into reuse that hits while still resident. Tile size selection is a cost-model problem tied to the target cache hierarchy's capacity and associativity; choosing T too large reintroduces capacity misses, too small adds loop overhead and under-utilizes available locality. Tiling's legality constraints are again dependence-direction-vector-based, generalizing interchange's constraints to the block structure, and tiling is frequently combined with interchange (choosing both a beneficial loop order and a blocking factor) to maximize reuse of multiple arrays with conflicting preferred traversal orders — this joint search is exactly the problem the polyhedral model is built to solve systematically rather than through a sequence of discrete, hand-ordered pattern-matched transformations: representing loop nests with affine (or near-affine) bounds and subscripts as integer point sets described by systems of linear inequalities (polyhedra), representing dependences as dependence polyhedra relating source and sink iteration points, and using integer linear programming (as in the Pluto algorithm, and its implementation in Polly/LLVM or GCC's Graphite) to search the entire space of legal affine schedules at once for one simultaneously optimizing fusion, interchange, and tiling decisions according to a locality/parallelism cost objective, rather than applying each transformation as a separate greedy legality-checked rewrite.

## Loop unswitching

Loop unswitching hoists a conditional branch whose condition is loop-invariant (does not depend on any value computed inside the loop) out of the loop entirely, by duplicating the loop body into two versions — one for each branch outcome — each specialized with the condition resolved statically, wrapped by a single outer `if` that selects which loop version executes. This trades code size for eliminating a per-iteration branch (and, more importantly, often exposes further optimization opportunities within each specialized copy, since each copy's body is simpler without the dead branch, and may become vectorizable or more amenable to LICM/strength reduction where the original branchy version was not). The legality condition is simply invariance of the branch condition with respect to the loop; profitability is bounded by code-size growth, which compounds if unswitching is applied to nested loops with multiple invariant conditionals, so compilers impose a code-growth budget and may unswitch only the most profitable (most frequently executed, or most optimization-unlocking) conditionals.
